content: 1. Rows shaded in pink indicate that the recommendation or good practice statement is identical for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. In other rows, the wording of the recommendations differs for each population. 2. In a screen-and-treat approach using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test, WHO suggests treating women who test positive for HPV DNA among the general population of women. 3. In a screen, triage, and treat approach using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among the general population of women, WHO suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid), or cytology to triage women after a positive HPV DNA test. The choice of triage method should depend on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and available resources in each country. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 4. In a screen, triage, and treat approach using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among women living with HIV, WHO suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology to triage women after a positive HPV DNA test. The benefits, harms, and programmatic costs of the triage options are similar, so the choice of method will depend on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and resources in each country. This is a conditional recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 5. WHO suggests starting regular cervical cancer screening at the age of 25 years among women living with HIV. Evidence of low certainty indicates that there are likely to be only a small number of women living with HIV who develop cervical cancer before the age of 25. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 6. After the age of 50 years, WHO suggests stopping cervical cancer screening after two consecutive negative screening results consistent with the recommended regular screening intervals among both the general population of women and women living with HIV. Neither VIA nor ablative treatment is suitable for screening or treatment of women in whom the transformation zone is not visible. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 7. Priority should be given to screening women aged 30–49 years in the general population of women. This is a good practice statement. 8. WHO suggests a regular screening interval of every 5 to 10 years when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among the general population of women. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 9. WHO suggests a regular screening interval of every 3 to 5 years when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test among women living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 10. While transitioning to a program with a recommended regular screening interval, screening even just twice in a lifetime is beneficial among both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a good practice statement. 11. As programs introduce HPV DNA testing, this test should be used at the woman’s next routine screening date, regardless of the test used at prior screening. In existing programs where cytology or VIA is the primary screening test, rescreening with the same test should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational among both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a good practice statement. 12. Once a decision to treat a woman is made—whether from the general population of women or women living with HIV—it is good practice to treat as soon as possible, ideally within six months, to reduce the risk of loss to follow-up. However, in pregnant women, good practice includes deferring treatment until after pregnancy. This is a good practice statement. 13. WHO suggests using large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold knife conization (CKC) for women from the general population and women living with HIV who have histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). Loop excision may be preferred in women of reproductive age, in settings with greater availability of LLETZ, and by providers with greater expertise performing LLETZ. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. 14. WHO suggests using either of the following strategies for cervical cancer prevention among the general population of women: HPV DNA detection in a screen-and-treat approach starting at the age of 30 years with regular screening every 5 to 10 years. HPV DNA detection in a screen, triage, and treat approach starting at the age of 30 years with regular screening every 5 to 10 years. 15. WHO suggests using the following strategy for cervical cancer prevention among women living with HIV: HPV DNA detection in a screen, triage, and treat approach starting at the age of 25 years with regular screening every 3 to 5 years.
